pages.title: About the shop
pages.content:
Dog-Ear Books opened in a former haberdashery on Wren Street with three thousand books, two armchairs and a cat called Margin. The armchairs and the cat are still here; the books have multiplied.

We are a small team of readers who choose every title on our shelves. We write our recommendations by hand, run a book club and a children's story hour, and will happily order anything we do not stock, usually within two days.

What we believe

  • Every reader deserves a bookseller who knows their taste.
  • Children's books are literature, not a side table.
  • Prices should be fair to readers, authors and the shop.
  • Dog-earing a page is a sign of love, not damage.

We would rather sell you the right book than the most books.

Ruth & Callum, booksellers

posts.title: Our autumn reading list
posts.excerpt: Eight books for longer evenings, chosen by the people behind the counter.
posts.content:
When the evenings draw in, we reach for books with a bit of weight to them: novels you can live inside for a week, and non-fiction that makes you look at the world differently.

At the top of the pile is A Map of Small Hours, a warm, clever novel set in a Lisbon hotel after midnight. If you prefer your fiction quieter, Salt and Silence is a short, tense story of two brothers on a salt marsh that we have been pressing on customers since August.

For non-fiction, How Rivers Remember is our pick of the season: a year spent walking a single river from source to sea, written with such care that you can almost hear the water.

And for small readers, Pip and the Paper Moon has become the bedtime book of half the street. Pop in and we will add a handwritten recommendation card to every book on the list.

posts.title: In defence of the dog-ear
posts.excerpt: Why we named a shop after a folded page corner, and why we sell bookmarks anyway.
posts.content:
People sometimes ask, a little nervously, whether a bookshop called Dog-Ear Books disapproves of folding page corners. The answer is no. We love a dog-eared book. It means somebody stopped at exactly the right moment and wanted to come back.

Secondhand books with folded corners are small maps of a previous reader's attention. We once found a novel where every page with a description of food had been turned down, and we have thought kindly of that stranger ever since.

That said, we also sell a very nice brass bookmark, shaped like a folded corner, for the people who cannot bear to crease a page. Both camps are welcome here.

Whatever you use, the point is the same: books are for reading, carrying, lending and loving into softness. A pristine spine is a sad thing.

posts.title: Story hour turns five
posts.excerpt: Five years of Saturday mornings, two hundred and fifty stories and one very patient tortoise puppet.
posts.content:
Five years ago, three children and their grandparents sat on cushions in the back of the shop for our very first story hour. Last Saturday, we counted thirty-one, plus a dog.

We have read around two hundred and fifty books aloud in that time. The most requested by far is The Tortoise Who Ran, which we now perform with a tortoise puppet and a small skateboard, to considerable applause.

Story hour is free and always will be. It is the part of the week that reminds us why we opened a bookshop in the first place: to watch someone fall in love with a story.

To celebrate, we are hosting a birthday story hour on the first Saturday of November with cake, paper moons to make and a surprise guest author. Everyone is welcome.

products.name: The Lighthouse Keeper's Daughter
products.description:
On a tidal island off a northern coast, eleven-year-old Ada learns to tend the great lamp from her father, who is slowly losing his sight. When a ship runs aground in the worst storm in fifty years, she has one night to keep the light burning and decide who she can trust.

Okafor writes the sea like a character and grief like weather: something that passes, returns and changes the shape of the shore. A novel for anyone who has loved a place that is disappearing.

Paperback, 352 pages.
products.short_description: by Marguerite Okafor. A girl, a lamp and a storm that keeps coming back. Our book of the month.

reviews.author: Harriet
reviews.content: I read it in a single sitting and then went straight back to the first chapter. The storm scenes are extraordinary.

reviews.author: Owen
reviews.content: Beautifully written and very moving. The middle sags a little, but the ending more than makes up for it.

products.name: Salt and Silence
products.description:
When their mother dies, Erik and Jonah return to the salt pans where they grew up, to sell the land and leave. But the marsh has its own memory, and neither brother is quite ready to say what happened the summer they stopped speaking.

A spare, atmospheric novel in short chapters that reads like a held breath. Paperback, 224 pages.
products.short_description: by Tomas Rydell. Two estranged brothers return to the family salt marsh. Quiet, tense and unforgettable.

products.name: A Map of Small Hours
products.description:
Every night from eleven until seven, Bento keeps the desk of a faded hotel in Lisbon. The guests who cannot sleep come down to talk, and over one winter their stories begin to overlap in ways none of them expected.

Warm, funny and quietly devastating, this is a novel made of small hours and the people who fill them. Hardback, 400 pages.
products.short_description: by Ines Albuquerque. A night porter, a hotel of strangers and the stories they tell after midnight.

reviews.author: Priya
reviews.content: The kind of book you press into friends' hands. Bento is my favourite narrator of the year.

products.name: The Orchard Letters
products.description:
Restoring her late aunt's cider farm, Nell finds a tin of letters hidden in the rafters of the apple store. Written between two people who were never meant to meet, they tell a story her family has kept quiet for eighty years.

A dual-timeline novel with a big heart and a perfectly judged ending. Paperback, 336 pages.
products.short_description: by Clementine Hart. A bundle of letters found in an apple store reveals a wartime love affair.

products.name: How Rivers Remember
products.description:
Rivers keep records: in their gravel, their bends and the plants that grow on their banks. Amara Fenwick spent a year walking a single river from a spring on the moor to its estuary, reading those records and meeting the people who live alongside the water.

Part science, part travel, part plea, this is the most hopeful book about the environment we have read in years. Hardback, 288 pages, with maps.
products.short_description: by Dr. Amara Fenwick. A hydrologist follows one river from source to sea, and asks what we owe it.

reviews.author: Gwen
reviews.content: Changed the way I look at the stream behind our house. Clear, generous and full of wonder.

products.name: The Quiet Economy
products.description:
An economist goes looking for the value that never shows up in the figures: the neighbour who fixes bicycles, the library that lends drills, the market stall that has run for forty years on trust. What he finds is a hidden economy as large as the one we measure.

Accessible, surprising and full of good ideas to steal for your own street. Hardback, 320 pages.
products.short_description: by Samuel Achterberg. Repair cafés, tool libraries and the small institutions that hold a town together.

products.name: Field Notes on Birds
products.description:
Over twelve months, artist Rosalind Mere kept a sketchbook by her kitchen window and another in her coat pocket. This gorgeous book gathers her drawings and notes on sixty common birds, with tips on what to look and listen for in each season.

Clothbound hardback with a ribbon marker, 192 pages, full colour throughout.
products.short_description: by Rosalind Mere. A beautifully illustrated year of garden and hedgerow birds, sketched from life.

products.name: Pip and the Paper Moon
products.description:
When the real moon hides behind the clouds, Pip the mouse cuts, folds and glues a moon of her own so that her friend Badger can fall asleep. A gentle bedtime story about kindness and making things, with lovely cut-paper illustrations.

Paperback picture book, 32 pages. Ages 3–6.
products.short_description: by Lottie Brennan. A little mouse builds a moon out of paper for her friend who is afraid of the dark.

reviews.author: Leo
reviews.content: Requested every single night for a month. The pictures are wonderful.

products.name: The Tortoise Who Ran
products.description:
Tilly has had enough of being told she is slow, so she enters the Great Meadow Race with a secret plan, a borrowed skateboard and absolutely no idea how to stop. Short chapters, big laughs and illustrations on every spread.

Paperback, 96 pages. Ages 6–9.
products.short_description: by Barnaby Quill. Tilly the tortoise is tired of being slow. A very funny first chapter book.

products.name: Linen Notebook
products.description:
Bound by hand in a small bindery, this lay-flat notebook has a linen cloth cover, a ribbon marker and 160 pages of 100 gsm cream paper with faint dot grid. It takes ink beautifully without bleeding through.

Choose oxblood, navy or mustard.
products.short_description: An A5 notebook bound in cloth, with 160 pages of cream, fountain-pen friendly paper.

products.name: Brass Bookmark
products.description: Etched brass that ages to a soft gold, shaped like a folded page corner so it hooks gently over the top of the page. No more dog-ears, unless you want them.
products.short_description: A slim brass bookmark with a cut-out dog-ear corner that clips over the page.

products.name: The Glass Orchard (e-book)
products.description:
Set the winter after the war, this novella follows the letter-writers of The Orchard Letters as they meet at last, in a greenhouse full of frost. A short, luminous read.

DRM-free EPUB and PDF, available to download from your account straight after purchase. Nothing is posted.
products.short_description: by Clementine Hart. The companion novella to The Orchard Letters, as a DRM-free e-book.
